passages.title: Inside the echo chamber
passages.text: Never before have citizens had access to so much information, and rarely have they agreed so little about what is true. Social media platforms show each user the content they are most likely to engage with, which often means content that confirms what they already believe. Over time, many people end up in an echo chamber, where opposing views are either absent or presented only to be mocked. The consequences for democracy are serious. Not only does constant exposure to one side of a debate harden people's opinions, but it also makes compromise look like betrayal. Politicians, aware of this, are increasingly tempted to speak only to their own supporters. The result is a polarized society in which the two sides no longer share even a basic set of facts. Little did the founders of these platforms imagine that their tools would one day shape elections. Some experts believe that stricter regulation is the answer; others argue that it would give governments too much control over speech. What most agree on is that media literacy, the ability to recognize bias and check sources, has never been more important.

passages.title: Watchdogs
passages.text: A free press is often described as the watchdog of democracy. Its role is not merely to report what those in power say, but to hold them accountable for what they do. Investigative journalists spend months, sometimes years, examining documents and interviewing sources before a story is published. When a transport minister was alleged to have awarded contracts to a friend's company, it was a small local newspaper, not a national broadcaster, that first revealed the story. The minister denied any wrongdoing, but the public scrutiny that followed eventually forced him to resign. Such cases appear to show that journalism still works. Yet the economic model that supports it is under pressure. As advertising has moved online, many local newspapers have closed, and those that remain tend to have fewer reporters. It could be argued that this leaves whole regions without anyone to ask difficult questions. Editors face a further dilemma. Readers increasingly expect publications to take sides, and outlets that try to sit on the fence risk being accused of cowardice by both camps. Balancing fairness and courage has always been hard; it is unlikely to get easier.
